title: NAACA: Training-Free NeuroAuditory Attentive Cognitive Architecture with Oscillatory Working Memory for Salience-Driven Attention Gating
one_liner: The paper adds a lightweight audio gate in front of a large audio-language model so the expensive model wakes up mainly when the sound stream shows a strong state change.
lead: Long audio recordings contain many stretches of routine background sound and a few short moments that matter: a scream, a crash, a siren, a sudden shift in crowd behavior. Sending every second of audio to a large audio-language model is costly and spreads focus across too much ordinary sound. This paper inserts a training-free front end that watches the sound stream for stable background patterns and sudden energy shifts. The large model is called mainly when that front end decides something important has changed, so the system spends its heavy reasoning budget on the moments that are most likely to matter.

problem.h2: Important audio events get buried in long recordings
paras: Audio understanding systems often process long clips where most of the signal is routine background: traffic hum, room tone, wind, distant chatter. Rare events are the part a user cares about, but they occupy only a small fraction of the recording.

If you run a large audio-language model on the whole recording evenly, the model spends as much effort on routine background as on the event of interest. That hurts twice. First, computation is wasted. Second, rare events get diluted because the system keeps revisiting the dominant background pattern instead of highlighting the moments where the sound state actually changed.

callout.html: Long recordings are dominated by ordinary background sound, so a large audio model wastes compute and focus unless something upstream decides when the recording became interesting.

steps.b: Read the audio stream over time
steps.text: Break the recording into short windows and summarize each window's current sound energy pattern.
Keep a running internal state that reflects the recent stable sound pattern.

steps.b: Measure mismatch between new sound and remembered sound
steps.text: Large mismatch means the current window is not just more of the same background.

steps.b: Open the gate when mismatch is high
steps.text: Call the large audio-language model mainly when the mismatch crosses a threshold.
After each window, refresh the memory so the gate tracks the new background if the environment has changed.

paras: The paper does not retrain the large audio-language model. Instead, it changes when that model is invoked. The new object is a front-end working-memory gate that filters a long audio stream and forwards only the windows judged salient enough to need deeper processing.
object.object: the salience gate in front of the audio-language model

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: salience energy gap
hidden.name: difference between current sound energy and remembered sound state
paras: The front end needs one core number: how far is the current audio window from the remembered background state? If the distance is small, the new window is probably routine continuation. If the distance is large, something changed in a way that may matter.

This quantity is useful because it ties focus to change, not just volume. A loud but steady background can become uninteresting after the memory settles to it. A quieter but unusual shift can still trigger the gate because it moves the state away from what the memory expected.

heat.caption: Darker means a larger departure from the remembered background state; bordered cells are the windows most likely to open the gate.

reads.html: The system asks whether the sound just became different enough from the recent background that it should allocate deeper processing.
The gate tracks adaptive energy fluctuations around an oscillatory working-memory state and invokes higher-level processing when the current window departs strongly from that state.

mechanism.h2: Why the gate helps long-form audio understanding
paras: Long recordings are repetitive. Once the system has learned the current background state, reprocessing every similar window adds little information. The working-memory gate cuts those windows away, which saves compute because the downstream model is no longer called on each routine segment.

The method also improves precision because the downstream model receives a cleaner stream of candidate events. When the input queue contains fewer routine windows, the event windows occupy a larger share of the model's processing budget. That raises the chance that rare but important events are kept rather than washed out by background repetition.

The training-free part matters operationally. You can place this gate in front of an existing audio-language model without collecting new labels or changing the model's weights. That is why the paper can report fewer unnecessary downstream calls together with better average precision: the gate changes which windows are examined deeply, and it does so by reacting to state change in the signal.

stages.s: Long audio stream cut into short windows
Maintain a working state for the recent background
Compare the new window to the current state
If the gap is high, open the gate and call the large audio model
If the gap is low, skip the heavy call and keep listening
Focused event detections with fewer expensive model calls

math.words: At each time step, compare the current audio summary to the remembered state. If the distance is larger than a threshold, trigger the large model. Otherwise keep listening and update memory quietly.
math.equation: gate_t = 1 if distance(current_window_t, memory_state_t) > threshold else 0
symbols: whether the large audio-language model is called at time t
summary of the current short audio window
working-memory state that represents recent background sound
how different the current window is from the remembered state
the minimum difference needed to treat the window as salient

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the remembered background state is steady street noise.
Window 1: same street noise, distance = 0.12. Threshold = 0.40. Gate = 0, so the large model is skipped.
Window 2: same street noise plus a faint pause, distance = 0.24. Gate = 0 again, because the change is still small.
Window 3: tire screech and impact, distance = 0.91. Gate = 1, so the large model is called.
Window 4: the new background settles to sirens and crowd noise. The memory updates so later similar siren windows are not all treated as fresh events.
This saves downstream calls because only windows whose state gap crosses the threshold trigger deeper processing.

math.note: The core decision is a threshold on state change. The paper's contribution is to make that state stable enough that routine sound stays quiet while event windows still stand out.

bars.h2: What the gate changes in practice

charts.title: Large model on every window
charts.note: The model sees everything, but rare events still get diluted because routine background occupies most of the compute.

charts.title: NAACA gate before the large model
charts.note: Precision improves because the gate forwards windows with strong state change, and cost drops because routine windows are filtered out.

items.html: If the threshold is set too high, subtle but important events never open the gate. This hurts recall because the large model never gets the chance to inspect those windows.
If the threshold is too low, many routine fluctuations trigger the gate. Then the system loses its compute savings because background noise is treated as salient.

If the working state does not update when the environment genuinely changes, the gate can keep firing on a new stable background. That wastes calls because the system mistakes a settled new context for a repeated fresh event.

Use a memory update rule that tracks genuine background changes and a threshold that preserves rare events. Then the gate helps because the large model spends its effort on intervals where the sound state moved enough to matter.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy audio monitor with synthetic long clips: steady background, then a few short event bursts. Maintain a running background state over windowed energy summaries. Trigger an expensive classifier only when the current window differs strongly from the background state. Compare this to a baseline that calls the classifier on every window.
demo.metric_eq: event_precision = true_event_windows_found / all_windows_flagged and call_rate = heavy_model_calls / total_windows
demo.closing: The demo should show that event precision rises while call rate falls, because the gate forwards windows whose state differs from the recent background instead of forwarding the full recording evenly.
